Miami's bar scene is undergoing a refined transformation, with a fresh generation of establishments championing vermouth and sherry-based cocktails alongside traditional Spanish drinks. According to Eater Miami, these new venues are capitalizing on the city's unique position as a gateway between the United States, the Caribbean, and Latin America—a cultural and geographic advantage that has long made Miami a champion of diverse flavors, from rum and agave spirits mingling with citrus to more exotic fruit-forward preparations.

Vermouth, an Italian aromatized fortified wine flavored with various botanicals, emerged in its modern form during the mid- to late 18th century in Turin, Italy, and has since become a cornerstone of classic cocktail culture. The spirit is now experiencing a renaissance in Miami's bar community, where bartenders are pairing vermouth with local ingredients and drawing on the city's multicultural heritage to craft drinks that feel both rooted in tradition and distinctly Floridian.

This shift toward vermouth and sherry represents more than a passing trend. It reflects a deliberate move away from the tropical-leaning cocktails that have long defined Miami's drinking culture. While rum and agave spirits will undoubtedly remain central to the city's bar identity, the new establishments are offering patrons a more expansive aperitif experience—one that honors European bartending traditions while remaining anchored to Miami's Caribbean and Latin American influences.

The city itself provides fertile ground for this evolution. As the second-most populous city proper in Florida with 442,241 residents, Miami attracts a sophisticated dining and drinking audience with access to international ingredients and culinary expertise. The broader South Florida metropolitan area, home to an estimated 6.39 million residents, further supports the kind of diverse bar culture that can sustain multiple concepts simultaneously.

These new bars are not rejecting Miami's established spirits vocabulary but rather expanding it. Classic Spanish cocktails—drinks with deep historical roots in Iberian bartending—are finding new life in venues designed around vermouth and sherry service. The result is a more nuanced cocktail landscape, one that acknowledges Miami's role as a cosmopolitan hub while celebrating the tropical and Latin American traditions that have always defined the city's flavor profile.

title: Miami Spice Back with New Reserve Tier and 300 Restaurants
summary: The 25th edition of Miami Spice Restaurant Months is back from August 1 through September 30, 2026. This year’s program from The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau (GMCVB) features three-course prix-fixe menus at a minimum of 30% savings at more than 300 participating…
whatHappening: Miami Spice Restaurant Month is returning for its 25th year, running August 1 through September 30, 2026. The program now features a new reserve tier and includes more than 300 participating restaurants offering three-course prix-fixe menus at a minimum of 30% savings.
whoInvolved: The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau (GMCVB) is organizing the program. The GMCVB is Miami's official destination marketing organization responsible for promoting tourism and cultural events across the region.
whyMatters: The expansion to over 300 restaurants and introduction of a reserve tier signals growing participation and sophistication in Miami's dining promotion efforts, making fine dining more accessible to a broader audience during the two-month window. For the hospitality industry, the program drives traffic during the late summer season and positions Miami as a competitive culinary destination.
articleBody:
Miami's signature dining promotion returns this summer with its most expansive lineup yet. According to Miami Curated, the 25th edition of Miami Spice Restaurant Month runs from August 1 through September 30, 2026, featuring three-course prix-fixe menus at participating establishments with savings of at least 30 percent. The program, organized by The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau, now encompasses more than 300 restaurants—a significant expansion from previous years—and introduces a new reserve tier to the traditional tiered pricing structure.

Miami Spice has become one of the region's premier culinary events since its inception a quarter-century ago. The program was designed to showcase Miami's diverse dining scene while offering residents and visitors an opportunity to experience fine dining at accessible price points. By anchoring the promotion to a defined two-month window during the late summer season, the GMCVB creates a concentrated marketing push that benefits both established fine-dining establishments and emerging culinary venues.

The addition of a reserve tier this year reflects broader changes in how dining promotions operate in competitive markets. Rather than a one-size-fits-all pricing model, the tiered approach allows high-end restaurants to participate at price points aligned with their positioning while still offering meaningful discounts. This flexibility appears designed to attract luxury establishments that previously may have hesitated to join a mass-market promotion, broadening the caliber of cuisine available during the event window.

With more than 300 restaurants now participating, Miami Spice covers an unusually wide geographic and culinary range. The scale of participation underscores Miami's position as a major dining destination with infrastructure capable of supporting major promotional campaigns. For diners, the expanded roster means greater choice across price points, cuisines, and neighborhoods throughout the greater Miami area.

The timing of Miami Spice—positioned in the late summer and early fall—traditionally targets both local residents seeking summer entertainment and the leading edge of the fall tourism season. By the time the program concludes at the end of September, Miami's high season begins to ramp up, creating momentum heading into the busy winter months when tourism peaks.

The 25th edition of Miami Spice opens registration for participating restaurants and begins accepting reservations from diners on August 1, 2026.

The Miami establishments highlighted in the guide suggest there remains an audience for spaces designed around classical principles of elegance, where attention to detail, ambiance, and tradition shape the guest experience.

For Miami's hospitality industry, the guide underscores continued demand from patrons seeking venues that offer an alternative to casual dining and drinking culture. These bars represent not nostalgia but an intentional choice to preserve standards of refined hospitality that appeal to travelers and residents willing to invest in a more elaborate evening experience.

articleBody:
Paperfish Sushi Brickell has long served as a dependable destination for casual meals and happy hour gatherings in Miami's Brickell neighborhood. However, the restaurant is now making a deliberate push to establish itself as a serious dinner venue, recognizing both an opportunity and a necessity in a market saturated with sushi options. According to Miami Curated, what has always set Paperfish apart is its inviting atmosphere—the lovely décor that brightens guests' moods the moment they enter—combined with consistent quality that keeps regulars returning with friends.

The sushi restaurant landscape in Miami is notably competitive, with numerous establishments vying for customer attention across all dayparts. In this crowded field, simply being reliable at lunch and happy hour is insufficient for long-term growth. Paperfish's strategic shift toward dinner service represents a recognition that the same design and quality strengths that attract midday crowds and after-work patrons can be leveraged to compete for evening diners willing to spend more per person.

The restaurant's approach appears to center on emphasizing its existing assets rather than wholesale reinvention. The décor that has always been a draw remains a cornerstone of the pitch, suggesting the upgrade is more about positioning and service evolution than physical transformation. This is a practical strategy for a restaurant that has already achieved product-market fit in its original dayparts but recognizes the untapped potential of the dinner segment.

For regulars who have enjoyed Paperfish as a casual spot, this transition raises questions about whether the dining experience will fundamentally change or whether the restaurant will simply extend its existing formula into evening hours. Many successful restaurants manage multiple dayparts by maintaining consistent quality while adjusting pricing and presentation slightly for different occasions—a model Paperfish appears to be testing.

The competitive pressure on sushi restaurants in Miami reflects broader trends in the restaurant industry, where venues must maximize revenue across all available hours. For Paperfish, stepping up its game at dinner service is a natural evolution that capitalizes on brand loyalty and physical assets already in place. Whether this expansion succeeds will likely depend on the restaurant's ability to execute the dinner experience at a level that matches guest expectations while preserving the qualities that made it a lunch favorite.
